answer:
Las siete nubes son las **Ananei HaKavod** (*עַנְנֵי הַכָּבוֹד*, "Nubes de Gloria") que según el Midrash acompañaron a Israel en el desierto: cuatro nubes a los cuatro costados, una encima, una debajo y una que iba delante del pueblo. Esta enumeración viene de la tradición midrásica (basada en mi conocimiento, no en los pasajes recuperados). Las fuentes recuperadas hablan de otros temas, aunque se relacionan de forma indirecta.

## Key Takeaways

- Las nubes protegían a Israel del calor, de los enemigos y de los animales peligrosos del desierto.
- Según la enumeración más conocida, cuatro rodeaban el campamento, una cubría desde arriba, una sostenía desde abajo y una guiaba al frente.
- La que iba delante allanaba el camino: bajaba las montañas, elevaba los valles y mataba serpientes y escorpiones.
- Hay otras versiones, con cinco o más nubes, y una discusión talmúdica sobre si fueron nubes literales o *sukkot* reales.
- Las fuentes recuperadas (Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer y Tosefta Sotah) no enumeran las nubes, pero aportan contexto sobre los ángeles y la medida de la bondad divina.

## Las siete nubes según el Midrash

La fuente bíblica es la columna de nube que guiaba a Israel de día (Éxodo 13:21) y el versículo "y la nube de Hashem estaba sobre ellos de día" (Números 10:34). El Midrash (Mejilta, Sifré y Yalkut Shimoni, según recuerdo) deduce que no era una sola nube, sino varias:

- **Cuatro nubes**, una en cada costado (este, oeste, norte y sur), que protegían de los enemigos y de las bestias.
- **Una nube arriba**, que daba sombra y protegía del sol y de la lluvia.
- **Una nube abajo**, que sostenía al pueblo y evitaba que la tierra los dañara.
- **Una nube delante**, que iba al frente para guiar el camino, nivelaba el terreno y eliminaba serpientes y escorpiones.

Algunas versiones cuentan la columna de fuego nocturna aparte o distribuyen las nubes de otra manera. Por eso conviene verificar la fuente exacta con un texto en mano. Otras tradiciones hablan de cinco nubes, y el Zohar tiene su propia lectura.

## ¿Nubes literales o sukkot?

El Talmud discute el sentido de "en sukkot habitaron los hijos de Israel" (Levítico 23:43) en [Sucá 11b]. Rabí Eliezer sostiene que se refiere a las nubes de gloria, mientras que Rabí Akiva dice que fueron sukkot reales. Por eso la fiesta de Sucot evoca esas nubes, que la tradición asocia al mérito de Aarón. Se dice que desaparecieron con su muerte y regresaron por el mérito de Moisés.

## Conexión con las fuentes recuperadas

**Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 4:3** describe la corte celestial: cuatro campamentos de ángeles (Mijael a la derecha, Gabriel a la izquierda, Uriel delante y Rafael detrás) con la Presencia Divina en el centro. La imagen es parecida a la de las nubes, porque Israel en el desierto, rodeado por cuatro lados por la gloria divina, refleja ese orden celestial. Esto es una asociación temática mía, no algo que el texto afirme.

**Tosefta Sotah 4:1** enseña que la medida de bondad divina supera a la de castigo en una proporción de uno a quinientos, y que Dios actúa "medida por medida". Abraham corrió para atender a los ángeles, y el Santo, bendito sea, "corrió" por sus hijos tres veces (Sinaí, Seír y Parán). Las nubes se suelen entender como parte de esa retribución: la hospitalidad de Abraham, que ofreció sombra bajo el árbol, se devuelve a sus hijos con sombra en el desierto. La conexión es temática, no explícita en el pasaje citado.

answer:
## תשובה ישירה

הקטעים שנשלפו אינם כוללים את ירושלמי ברכות פרק ה׳ דף ט׳ ע״ב, ולכן איני יכול לצטט ממנו לשון מדויקת. לפי מבנה הדפוס, ההפניה הזו נופלת כנראה בתוך פרק "אין עומדין" (פרק ה׳), העוסק בכובד ראש בתפילה, בהזכרת גבורות גשמים ובשאלת "טעות בתפילה". הדפדוף בירושלמי הוא בעמודות (א–ד), ולכן ייתכן שההפניה שלך היא לעמודה ולא לעמוד. כדאי לוודא באיזו מהדורה מדובר (וילנא, ונציה או ספריא).

## נקודות עיקריות

- **פרק ה׳** נפתח במשנה "אין עומדין להתפלל אלא מתוך כובד ראש", והירושלמי דן במשמעות כובד הראש ובדרך החסידים הראשונים.
- **הנושאים המרכזיים בפרק:** הזכרת גבורות גשמים ו"שאלת גשמים", דין המאריך או המקצר בתפילה, ו"המתפלל וטעה".
- **סוגיות רחבות יותר:** הירושלמי מרבה בשאלות של כוונה ושל דרך ההתייחסות לתפילה כעמידה לפני מלך.
- **הקטעים שנשלפו** מראים את דרכו של הירושלמי כמקור לראשונים, אך אינם עוסקים בפרק ה׳.

## פירוט

### מה שמבוסס על הקטעים שנשלפו

הקטעים שהובאו מזכירים את הירושלמי במקומות אחרים בברכות:

- **רש״י על ברכות ד ע״ב** מביא את הירושלמי בעניין סמיכת גאולה לתפילה, במשל על "אוהבו של מלך" שדפק על הפתח ומצא שהמלך הפליג. כאן הירושלמי מהווה יסוד לדין סמיכת גאולה לתפילה [Rashi, Berakhot 4b, citing Yerushalmi Berakhot].
- **רש״י על ברכות ב ע״א** והרא״ש (פרק א׳) מביאים את הירושלמי: הקורא קריאת שמע לפני זמנה לא יצא, ולכן קריאתה בבית הכנסת נועדה "לעמוד בתפילה מתוך דברי תורה" [Rosh, Berakhot 1:1].
- **מי השלוח** מביא את הירושלמי ברכות א:ה על העין כ"סירסור ללב" [Mei HaShiloach, Kedoshim].
- **העמק דבר** מביא את ירושלמי ברכות ט:ג, "אמנו רחל מנביאות" [Haamek Davar, Genesis 30:23].

### מה שמבוסס על ידיעתי הכללית (ללא ציטוט מדויק)

פרק ה׳ נפתח במשנה על כובד ראש. הגמרא הבבלית מזכירה שם את החסידים הראשונים ש"היו שוהין שעה אחת ומתפללין" [Berakhot 30b]. הירושלמי עוסק שם באותו עניין, וגם בהלכות כמו "הזכרת גבורות גשמים". מטבע הדברים, ההבדלים בין הבבלי לירושלמי בעניינים אלה הם מהחלקים המעניינים בלימוד הפרק.

לא אנסה לשחזר מתוך הזיכרון את הסוגיה המדויקת שבעמוד זה, כדי לא לייחס לירושלמי דברים שלא נאמרו בו.

### איך נמשיך

- אם תדביק כאן את הטקסט של העמוד, או תגיד באיזו הלכה מדובר (למשל ה״ב או ה״ג), אלמד אותו איתך שורה אחר שורה, עם פירושי **קרבן העדה** ו**פני משה**.
- אפשר גם לבחור נושא מהפרק (כובד ראש, גבורות גשמים, טעות בתפילה) ולהשוות לסוגיה המקבילה בבבלי.

Главный спор на Шаббат 97б связан с вопросом, виновен ли человек в переносе (*hotzaah*), если предмет пролетел по воздуху из одного общественного владения (*reshut harabim*) в другое через частное владение между ними. Согласно Мишне, **рабби Акива** признаёт его виновным, а **мудрецы** освобождают. Ниже пересказ по памяти, и я не уверен в каждой детали, поэтому сверяйтесь с текстом. Если вы имели в виду другой сюжет этой страницы, уточните.

## Key Takeaways

- Спор касается броска или переноса через частное владение, которое лежит между двумя общественными.
- Рабби Акива: виновен, мудрецы: свободен (по Мишне, трактат Шаббат).
- Рамбам постановляет, что человек виновен, если сумма пути в двух общественных владениях составляет более четырёх локтей, а предмет не остановился в промежуточном владении [Mishneh Torah, Sabbath 13:17, со ссылкой на Шаббат 97б–98а].
- Рядом обсуждается роль намерения (*kavana*): для виновности работа должна совпасть с задуманным [Mishneh Torah, Sabbath 1:8; 13:21].
- Предыдущий лист (96б–97а) содержит знаменитый спор рабби Акивы и рабби Йегуды бен Бетейры о «собирателе дров».

## Подробнее

### Суть спора (пшат)

Основа запрета переноса в том, что предмет должен быть поднят (*akira*) из одного владения и положен (*hanacha*) в другом. Минимальная дистанция в общественном владении составляет четыре локтя.

В нашем случае между двумя общественными владениями находится частное. Предмет пролетает над ним и не останавливается. Возникает вопрос, считать ли пройденное расстояние единым или разорванным.

### Позиция Рамбама

Рамбам объясняет, что виновность наступает, потому что четыре локтя набираются сложением пути в обоих общественных владениях. Предмет не остановился в промежуточном владении, и поэтому нет разрыва [Mishneh Torah, Sabbath 13:17]. Источником он называет Шаббат 97б–98а.

### Намерение (*kavana*)

С этим связаны два принципа из Рамбама:

- Если человек хотел совершить одну запрещённую работу, а совершил другую, которую не имел в виду, он не виновен, потому что его намерение не исполнилось [Mishneh Torah, Sabbath 1:8].
- Если он хотел бросить предмет на восемь локтей, а тот упал чуть дальше четырёх, он виновен. Предмет не может пролететь восемь локтей, не пройдя через каждую точку этой дистанции, поэтому намерение отчасти исполнилось [Mishneh Torah, Sabbath 13:21].

*Эти пункты взяты из предоставленных источников. Описание самого спора рабби Акивы и мудрецов основано на моих знаниях.*

### Связь с темой «мудрецы спорили»

Мишна в Пиркей Авот различает два вида разногласий. Спор ради Небес, как у Гилеля и Шамая, будет иметь продолжение, а спор Кораха и его общины не будет [Pirkei Avot 5:17]. Споры рабби Акивы и мудрецов в Шаббате относятся к первому виду.

Для практических вопросов обратитесь к местному раввину или галахическому авторитету (*posek*).

answer:
Je ne peux pas dessiner d'image, mais voici une illustration en mots et en schéma du **chapitre 6 de Yoma** (*Shnei Se'irei*, « les deux boucs », [Yoma 62a ss.]). Ce chapitre décrit le rite des deux boucs de Yom Kippour : le tirage au sort, l'aveu du Cohen Gadol, puis l'envoi du bouc vers le désert (*Azazel*). Si vous pensiez à un autre type d'illustration (dessin, tableau, résumé), précisez-le.

## Key Takeaways

- Les deux boucs doivent être semblables en apparence, taille et valeur [Mishna Yoma 6:1].
- Le sort désigne un bouc « *LaHashem* » (sacrifié) et l'autre « *LaAzazel* » (envoyé).
- Le Cohen Gadol confesse les fautes sur le bouc émissaire, qui est conduit hors de Jérusalem.
- Le bouc est précipité d'un rocher, et un signal avertit Jérusalem que le rite est accompli.
- Le thème central est la *teshouva* (repentir) et le pardon divin, comme dans Jonas 3:10.

## Illustration : la scène

*Cette reconstitution suit la Mishna ; les détails viennent de ma connaissance de la tradition, non du passage récupéré.*

```
TEMPLE (Azara)                          DÉSERT
 ┌─────────────────────┐
 │ Cohen Gadol         │
 │ [urne] 2 sorts      │
 │  droite → "LaHashem"│ → égorgé, sang porté au Saint des Saints
 │  gauche → "LaAzazel"│ → fil d'écarlate sur la tête
 └─────────────────────┘
        │ aveu (vidouï) sur le bouc
        ▼
  Jérusalem ── 10 cabanes ── ... ── dernière cabane ── Tsouk (falaise)
   (notables      « voici nourriture      │              │
   accompagnent)   et eau »               ▼              ▼
                                   l'homme désigné    bouc précipité
                                   (*ish iti*)        en arrière
```

## Les étapes

### 1. Deux boucs identiques
La Mishna exige que les deux boucs soient semblables en apparence, en taille et en valeur, et achetés ensemble [Mishna Yoma 6:1]. Le Cohen Gadol tire deux sorts : l'un porte « pour l'Éternel », l'autre « pour Azazel » (cf. Lévitique 16:8).

### 2. Le fil d'écarlate et le vidouï
Le Cohen Gadol attache un fil de laine écarlate sur la tête du bouc émissaire. Il pose ensuite les mains sur le taureau et confesse ses fautes, celles de sa maison et des Cohanim. Quand il prononce le Nom, l'assistance répond : « *Baroukh shem kevod malkhouto léolam vaèd* » (« Béni soit le nom de la gloire de Sa royauté à jamais »).

### 3. Le trajet vers le désert
Un homme désigné, l'*ish iti*, conduit le bouc. Les notables de Jérusalem l'accompagnent, et dix cabanes jalonnent la route. À chacune on offre de la nourriture et de l'eau à l'homme. Les notables s'arrêtent à la dernière cabane et observent de loin.

### 4. La falaise
Arrivé au *Tsouk* (rocher abrupt), l'homme partage le fil : une moitié sur le rocher, l'autre entre les cornes du bouc. Il le pousse en arrière, et le bouc est mis en pièces avant d'avoir descendu la moitié de la pente. Des signaux avertissent alors Jérusalem.

## Sens et lien avec la teshouva

Le *pshat* est un rite d'expiation collective. Le Talmud en fait aussi un exemple de *'houkim* (décrets divins sans raison apparente) face aux critiques des nations, à la fin du chapitre [Yoma 67b]. La Torah dit : « Mes décrets, vous les garderez » (Lévitique 18:4).

Le texte de Jonas fourni (3:10-4:1) éclaire le thème : « Et Dieu vit leurs actes, car ils étaient revenus de leur mauvaise voie, et Dieu regretta le mal qu'Il avait dit leur faire, et ne le fit pas » (וַיַּרְא הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת־מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם כִּי־שָׁבוּ מִדַּרְכָּם הָרָעָה). Jonas est lu à Min'ha de Yom Kippour, mais ce lien vient de ma connaissance de la tradition, pas du chapitre de Yoma lui-même. Le renvoi du bouc et le repentir de Ninive illustrent tous deux l'idée que le pardon suit le retour sincère.

Souhaitez-vous un schéma plus détaillé d'une étape (par exemple le tirage au sort), ou l'analyse d'une discussion de la Guemara sur ce chapitre ?

# ברכות ב עמוד א: פתיחת המסכת

**התשובה הקצרה:** המשנה הראשונה במסכת ברכות פותחת בשאלה *"מאימתי קורין את שמע בערבין?"* וקובעת שזמן קריאת שמע של ערבית מתחיל "משעה שהכהנים נכנסים לאכול בתרומתן", כלומר מצאת הכוכבים. סופו של הזמן שנוי במחלוקת: עד סוף האשמורה הראשונה (ר' אליעזר), עד חצות (חכמים), או עד עלות השחר (רבן גמליאל). הגמרא שואלת מדוע המשנה פותחת דווקא בערבית ובסימן של כהנים, ומתרצת שהמשנה נשענת על הפסוק "בשכבך ובקומך".

*(אין מקורות שנשלפו לשאלה זו. הדברים להלן מבוססים על ידיעתי במסורת.)*

## נקודות עיקריות

- המשנה מתחילה בקריאת שמע של **ערבית** משום שהפסוק אומר "בשכבך" לפני "ובקומך" [דברים ו:ז].
- תחילת הזמן הוא "משעה שהכהנים נכנסים לאכול בתרומתן", כלומר צאת הכוכבים, שאז הכהן הטמא שטבל מותר בתרומה [ויקרא כב:ז].
- ר' אליעזר: עד סוף האשמורה הראשונה. חכמים: עד חצות. רבן גמליאל: עד עלות השחר.
- המשנה מסבירה ש"עד חצות" הוא **סייג** (הרחקה מן העבירה), ושמצוות רבות אחרות נמשכות עד עלות השחר.

## המשנה

המשנה מביאה מעשה: בניו של רבן גמליאל חזרו מבית המשתה ואמרו שלא קראו קריאת שמע. השיב להם שאם לא עלה עמוד השחר, חייבים הם לקרוא. הוא הוסיף שכל דבר שאמרו חכמים "עד חצות", מצוותו נמשכת עד עלות השחר, למשל הקטר חלבים ואברים ואכילת קרבנות הנאכלים ליום אחד.

המשנה שואלת: "אם כן, למה אמרו חכמים עד חצות?" ותשובתה: **"כדי להרחיק את האדם מן העבירה"**, שלא יישן ויחמיץ את הזמן.

## שאלות הגמרא בדף ב ע"א

### "תנא היכא קאי?"

הגמרא שואלת על מה נשענת המשנה כשהיא פותחת ב"מאימתי". תשובה אחת: **"תנא אקרא קאי"**, כלומר התנא מסתמך על הפסוק "בשכבך ובקומך", וכוונתו לברר מתי זמן "שכיבה". תשובה אחרת: הסדר נלמד מבריאת העולם, "ויהי ערב ויהי בקר" [בראשית א:ה], והלילה קודם ליום.

### "מאי שנא דתני בערבית ברישא?"

על פי התירוץ הראשון, התנא מקדים ערבית כסדר הפסוק. הגמרא מקשה אחר כך מדוע לא פתחה המשנה בשחרית, ואף מבררת מדוע נקט התנא את סימן הכהנים ולא פשוט "משעת צאת הכוכבים". התשובה היא שהמשנה מלמדת דין בדרך אגב: כהן שנטמא וטבל נעשה טהור לאכול בתרומה רק אחרי שקיעת החמה [ויקרא כב:ז], וכפרתו אינה מעכבת את אכילתו.

## מחלוקת התנאים: מדוע שלוש דעות?

- **ר' אליעזר** סובר שהלילה מחולק לשלוש משמרות, ולכן הזמן מסתיים בסוף הראשונה (הגמרא דנה בזה בדף ג).
- **חכמים** קובעים חצות, שהוא סייג שקבעו כדי שלא יידחה הדבר.
- **רבן גמליאל** מחזיק בדין התורה עצמו: זמן "בשכבך" נמשך כל הלילה עד עלות השחר.

ההבדל נעוץ בשאלה אם הזמן שקבעו חכמים הוא הגדרת הדין עצמו או גדר מרחיק. לפי המשנה, חכמים עצמם מודים שמן התורה הזמן נמשך עד עלות השחר, ו"עד חצות" נועד להרחיק מן העבירה.

## נושא רחב יותר

הפתיחה מלמדת עיקרון: הקשר בין זמן, מצווה וסייג. הגמרא ממשיכה בדפים הבאים לדון בשאלות אלה לעומק, ובהן מהות "אשמורות" ומשמעות עלות השחר.

**Cette Mishna (*Hagiga* 2:1) enseigne qu'il est inutile, voire dangereux, de spéculer sur ce qui dépasse les limites de l'intellect humain : ce qu'il y a au-dessus, en dessous, avant la Création et après la fin des temps.** Elle ajoute que celui qui ne se soucie pas de l'honneur de son Créateur aurait mieux fait de ne pas naître. Il s'agit d'une mise en garde contre l'arrogance intellectuelle et spirituelle, pas d'une interdiction de poser des questions.

*(Aucune source n'a été fournie pour cette question ; la réponse repose sur ma connaissance de la tradition.)*

## Points clés

- Le texte est tiré de la Mishna [Hagiga 2:1] et est développé dans [Hagiga 11b-16a].
- Les quatre choses sont : *ma lema'ala* (ce qui est au-dessus), *ma lematta* (ce qui est en dessous), *ma lefanim* (ce qui précède) et *ma le'achor* (ce qui suit).
- La Guemara et les commentateurs y voient une limite posée à la spéculation métaphysique et cosmologique.
- La seconde partie de la Mishna, sur « l'honneur du Créateur », relie la curiosité excessive au manque de respect envers D.ieu.
- La Torah elle-même encourage l'étude et la réflexion, mais dans un cadre précis.

## Le texte

מִי שֶׁהוּא מִסְתַּכֵּל בְּאַרְבָּעָה דְּבָרִים, רָאוּי לוֹ כְּאִלּוּ לֹא בָּא לָעוֹלָם: מַה לְּמַעְלָה, מַה לְּמַטָּה, מַה לְּפָנִים, וּמַה לְּאָחוֹר. וְכָל שֶׁלֹּא חָס עַל כְּבוֹד קוֹנוֹ, רָאוּי לוֹ שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לָעוֹלָם.

« Quiconque scrute quatre choses, il vaudrait mieux pour lui qu'il ne soit pas venu au monde : ce qui est en haut, ce qui est en bas, ce qui est avant, ce qui est après. Et quiconque ne ménage pas l'honneur de son Créateur, il vaudrait mieux pour lui qu'il ne soit pas venu au monde. » [Mishna Hagiga 2:1]

## Le sens simple (*pshat*)

Selon l'interprétation classique, on parle de spéculation sur :

- **Ce qui est en haut** : la nature des cieux et du monde céleste, au-delà de ce que révèle la Torah.
- **Ce qui est en bas** : ce qui se trouve sous la terre ou dans les profondeurs.
- **Ce qui précède** : ce qui existait avant la Création.
- **Ce qui suit** : ce qui se passera après la fin du monde.

Ces questions dépassent la capacité de l'esprit humain. Les poursuivre sans fondement mène à l'erreur, voire à l'hérésie.

## Le développement dans la Guemara

La Guemara [Hagiga 11b] cite un verset de Deutéronome 4:32 : « Interroge donc les temps anciens, depuis le jour où D.ieu créa l'homme sur la terre, et d'une extrémité des cieux à l'autre. » Elle en déduit qu'on peut s'interroger d'une extrémité à l'autre, mais pas sur ce qui est au-dessus, en dessous, avant ou après.

Elle cite aussi *Ben Sira* (d'après mon souvenir de ce passage) : « Ne cherche pas ce qui est trop merveilleux pour toi, ne sonde pas ce qui est trop caché pour toi ; médite sur ce qui t'est permis, et n'aie pas affaire aux choses cachées. »

## Le lien avec la Création : la lettre *Bet*

Le **Midrash** [Bereshit Rabba 1:10] explique pourquoi la Torah commence par la lettre *Bet* (ב) de *Bereshit*. Cette lettre est fermée sur trois côtés et ouverte vers l'avant. Comme elle, l'homme n'a pas à chercher ce qui est au-dessus, en dessous ou avant, mais doit regarder vers l'avant, à partir de la Création.

## La seconde partie : l'honneur du Créateur

La Guemara [Hagiga 11b et 16a] propose plusieurs explications de « celui qui ne ménage pas l'honneur de son Créateur ». Selon l'une d'elles, il s'agit de celui qui pèche en secret, comme si D.ieu ne voyait pas. Une autre mentionne celui qui regarde l'arc-en-ciel avec une curiosité déplacée. (Je cite ces opinions de mémoire ; vérifiez l'attribution exacte dans le texte.)

Le lien avec la première partie est la retenue devant la grandeur divine. La spéculation immodérée peut devenir un manque de respect.

## Les commentateurs

- **Rashi** reprend l'explication des quatre dimensions et souligne que la question vise ce qui précède la Création.
- **Maïmonide** (*Rambam*) insiste dans le *Guide des égarés* (I:31-32) sur les limites de l'intellect humain. Dans *Yesodei haTorah* (chap. 4), il traite de l'étude de la *Ma'asseh Bereshit* et de la *Ma'asseh Merkava*, réservée à des personnes préparées.
- **Nahmanide** (*Ramban*), sur Genèse 1:1, souligne que certains aspects de la Création sont cachés et transmis uniquement par tradition.

## Une interdiction de réfléchir ?

Non. La Torah encourage l'étude et la réflexion sur la Création, comme on le voit dans les Psaumes (« Que tes œuvres sont grandes, Éternel ! », Ps. 92:6). La Mishna vise surtout la spéculation sans cadre ni humilité, détachée de la tradition.

Le **Talmud de Jérusalem** et d'autres sources expliquent aussi que la mise en garde porte sur le fait de s'y plonger sans préparation. La tradition de la *Kabbale* traite ces thèmes, mais dans un cadre de transmission strict.

answer:
The retrieved text of **Kiddushin 32a** opens mid-discussion on a question about honoring parents: whose money pays for the expenses of *kibbud av va'em* (honoring father and mother)? The Gemara records a dispute between **Rav Yehuda** (from the son's resources) and **Rav Natan bar Oshaya** (from the father's resources). The rabbis ruled for Rav Yirmeya, or his son, according to the view of "from the father."

## Key Takeaways

- The central question is financial: who bears the cost of feeding, clothing, and caring for a parent?
- Rav Yehuda says the cost falls on the son; Rav Natan bar Oshaya says it comes from the father's own funds.
- The Gemara cites a parallel between "Honor your father" (Exodus 20:12) and "Honor the Lord with your wealth" (Proverbs 3:9) to argue that honor involves a cost to the person honoring.
- Even if the cost is the father's, the son still bears *bittul melacha* (loss of work time), so the parallel with a "loss to the pocket" still holds.
- Chasidic sources cite this daf for the teaching that a *zaken* (elder) is one who has acquired wisdom.

## The Text and Its Argument

### "Whose money?"

The Gemara asks: "מִשֶּׁל מִי?" (From whose [resources]?).

- **Rav Yehuda**: "מִשֶּׁל בֵּן", from the son's.
- **Rav Natan bar Oshaya**: "מִשֶּׁל אָב", from the father's.
- The rabbis instructed Rav Yirmeya (or his son) like the view of "from the father" [Kiddushin 32a].

### The challenge from a baraita

The Gemara raises an objection (*meitivei*, "they challenged"). The verse says "Honor your father and your mother," and elsewhere "Honor the Lord with your wealth." Just as honoring God involves *chesron kis* (a loss from one's pocket), so does honoring parents.

If the money comes from the father, what loss does the son bear? The Gemara answers: *bittul melacha*, the time he loses from his work in attending to his father [Kiddushin 32a].

The passage then begins to bring another proof ("Come and hear..."), about brothers, partners, and father and son. The retrieved text cuts off here, so I won't reconstruct the rest from it.

### Why the disagreement?

The dispute turns on what kind of obligation *kibbud* is. If it is an act-based duty, the son must absorb its costs. If it is a duty of service and not of funding, the parent's own assets cover the parent's needs, and the son contributes his time and effort.

## Practical Halacha

The ruling is codified in the **Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 240:5**, following the view that the father's own funds are used where he has them. The son may not let his father suffer or be humiliated, and the poskim discuss how far his obligation extends where the father has no means. These details are my own knowledge, not from the retrieved passages.

## Related Sources Retrieved

- **Torah Ohr, Mishpatim** and **Likkutei Torah, Tzav** (Chasidut) cite Kiddushin 32a, together with Bereishit Rabbah 59:9, for the teaching "איזהו זקן? שקנה חכמה" (Who is a *zaken*? One who has acquired wisdom). This connects to the daf's discussion of honoring elders and Torah scholars (Leviticus 19:32). The retrieved text gives only the citation, not the discussion itself.
- **Peninei Halakhah, Kashrut 13:8** discusses an Amora who feigned anger and broke a vessel to educate his household, which is permitted because he stayed in control. It concerns the prohibition of wanton destruction (*bal tashchit*) and the gravity of anger, not the content of this daf. It appears to be a thematic tangent on educating family members. The parallel story I know of is in Berachot 30b.

answer:
Bava Metzia 5a is about when a person must make a serious promise (an oath) in court after admitting part of a claim. The discussion asks why the Torah excludes **land** from that rule, since land can't be carried off or hidden like a toy. The page also brings a teaching that the four kinds of guardians have this same rule.

## Key Takeaways

- If someone says "I owe you some, but not all," the Torah makes him swear about the rest (*modeh b'miktzat*, partial admission).
- This oath applies to movable things, not land.
- One opinion says that if you can just say "Here it is, take it!" (*heilach*), you are exempt from the oath.
- That raises a question: if land is always "here," why did the Torah need a verse to exclude it?
- The Gemara answers with special cases: land that was changed (pits, ditches, caves), or a claim that mixes movables and land.
- Rami bar Chama then teaches that all four guardians (unpaid guardian, borrower, paid guardian, renter) have the partial-admission rule.

*Note: the retrieved text covers only the first part of this daf, up to the Rami bar Chama baraita, which cuts off mid-sentence. The ideas and kid-friendly analogies below beyond that point are my own explanation, not from the retrieved text. The other retrieved passages (Ibn Ezra, Ba'al HaTurim) are not about this daf.*

## The Story in Kid Language

### Setting the scene

Imagine your friend Dani says, "Yossi, you have 4 of my toy cars!" Yossi answers, "I have 2 of them, but not the other 2." Yossi admitted part and denied part.

The Torah says that in this situation Yossi must make a very serious promise, an oath, that he really doesn't have the other 2. This is the rule of *modeh b'miktzat*. The idea is that most people wouldn't lie when they have to swear in God's name.

### Why land is different

The Torah's oath is about things you can pick up and move, like toy cars, coins, or a coat. Land, like a backyard, can't be picked up or hidden. That is why land is excluded from this oath.

### The "Heilach" idea

*Heilach* is Aramaic for "Here, take it!" One opinion says that if someone can hand the thing right back, he doesn't need to swear.

The Gemara then asks the question of this page. If **everything about land is "heilach"** (the land is just sitting there), why did the Torah need a special verse to exclude land from the oath? [Bava Metzia 5a] The text says: "הָא כׇּל קַרְקַע הֵילָךְ הוּא", "But all land is *heilach*!"

### The Gemara's two answers

The Gemara replies that the verse is still needed in two situations: [Bava Metzia 5a]

1. **When he dug pits, ditches, and caves in it** (בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת). Now it's not exactly the land he took. It's like borrowing a flat sandbox and handing it back full of holes. He can't simply say "Here it is," yet the Torah still doesn't make him swear, because it is land.
2. **When someone claims both movables and land.** The defendant admits the movables (the toy cars) and denies the land (the backyard). A person might think the admission about the toys would make him swear about the yard too. The verse teaches that the land part doesn't get the oath.

### The four guardians

The Gemara then says "Come and hear" (*ta shma*), which means it is bringing a proof from a teaching of Rami bar Chama. He taught that four guardians need "denial of part and admission of part" for the oath: [Bava Metzia 5a]

- **Shomer chinam**: an unpaid guardian, like a friend who watches your toy for free.
- **Sho'el**: a borrower, who uses your toy.
- **Noseh sachar**: a paid guardian, who is paid to watch it.
- **Socher**: a renter, who pays to use it.

The Gemara then starts to ask what exactly the case is. The text cuts off at "הֵיכִי דָּמֵי? לָאו…" ("What is the case? Is it not…"). The rest of the discussion isn't in the retrieved text.

## Why the Gemara Cares

The Gemara is not only collecting rules. It asks "Why do we need this?" about every verse and every rule.

If a verse seems unnecessary, the sages look for the special case where it teaches something new. That is why the pits, ditches, and caves appear. This also reflects a theme in the Torah: land holds a special status. As Leviticus 25:23 says, "וְהָאָרֶץ לֹא תִמָּכֵר לִצְמִתֻת, כִּי לִי הָאָרֶץ" ("The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is Mine"). This verse is not cited in the Gemara here. I mention it only as a loosely related idea, not as the Gemara's source.

## A Simple Picture to Remember

- **Toys** can be moved or hidden, so partial denial needs an oath.
- **Land** stays put, so no oath.
- **"Heilach"** means "Here, take it!"
- **Four guardians** (free, borrower, paid, renter) all follow the partial-admission rule.

answer:
Chullin 80a continues the Gemara's discussion of hybrid animals, specifically whether an animal born of two species counts as a *seh* (small livestock, sheep or goat) for various laws. The **Rabbanan** hold that "seh" includes even a partial seh, while **Rabbi Eliezer** holds that it does not. **Rav Pappa** then draws a practical conclusion about which laws can apply to such hybrids. The retrieved passage cuts off mid-discussion, so I summarize only what it contains and note where I am supplementing.

## Key Takeaways

- The Rabbanan and Rabbi Eliezer dispute whether "seh" includes a partial seh, such as a hybrid.
- Rav Pappa says that for both *kisui ha-dam* (covering blood) and *matanot* (priestly gifts), the only case where both laws apply is a deer (*tzvi*) that mated with a she-goat (*te'ishah*).
- In that case, both sides are uncertain whether we take the father's seed into account (*zera ha-av*).
- For *oto ve'et beno* (not slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day), the passage begins to list further hybrid cases, but the text is cut off.

## Detailed Discussion

### The core dispute: what counts as a "seh"?

The passage opens with the phrase "בְּשֶׂה וַאֲפִילּוּ מִקְצָת שֶׂה" ("[the verse says] 'seh,' even a partial seh"). [Chullin 80a]

- **The Rabbanan** read "seh" broadly: it includes even an animal that is only partly a seh, meaning a hybrid.
- **Rabbi Eliezer** reads it narrowly: "seh" means a full seh, not a partial one.

The question is whether a verse that names a species also covers mixed-species offspring.

### Rav Pappa's conclusion

Rav Pappa states: "הִלְכָּךְ, לְעִנְיַן כִּסּוּי הַדָּם וּמַתָּנוֹת, לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ אֶלָּא בִּצְבִי הַבָּא עַל הַתְּיָישָׁה" ("Therefore, regarding covering the blood and the priestly gifts, you only find [both applying] in the case of a deer that mated with a she-goat"). [Chullin 80a]

The reason given is that "between the Rabbanan and Rabbi Eliezer, they are uncertain whether we are concerned for the father's seed or not." The two sides then differ only on the question of "seh and even part of a seh."

My explanation, from general knowledge of the sugya (not from the retrieved text):

- *Kisui ha-dam* applies to a *chayah* (wild animal) or bird. *Matanot* apply to domesticated animals.
- A hybrid of a wild father (deer) and a domestic mother (goat) sits between the two categories.
- Because it is uncertain whether the father's species determines the animal's status, both obligations can arise in this one case.

### Oto ve'et beno

The passage then turns to *oto ve'et beno*, the prohibition against slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day [Leviticus 22:28]. It begins: "לְעִנְיַן אוֹתוֹ וְאֶת בְּנוֹ, מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ בֵּין בְּתַיִישׁ הַבָ..." ("Regarding *oto ve'et beno*, you find it both in a [male] goat that…"). The text breaks off here, so I cannot reliably report the cases or conclusions that follow.

### Sources note

- **From the retrieved passage:** the Rabbanan and Rabbi Eliezer dispute, Rav Pappa's statement, and the uncertainty about the father's seed.
- **From my general knowledge:** the explanation of why the deer-and-goat case triggers both laws. Please check this against the full text of the daf and Rashi.

answer:
The Gemara you mean is most likely **Yoma 57a**, where R. Elazar son of R. Shimon says he saw the *paroches* (the curtain) in Rome with drops of blood on it. The retrieved passages don't contain this sugya or the Tosafot, so what follows is from my own knowledge, and I can't quote the Tosafot's exact wording. If the paroches was from the First Temple, the simplest answer is that Babylon's plunder was not the end of the story. **Cyrus returned the Temple vessels** (Ezra 1:7-11), so a First Temple paroches could have been reused in the Second Temple and later taken by Titus.

## Key Takeaways
- The question assumes Nebuchadnezzar's plunder removed everything permanently, but the vessels were later returned.
- Ezra records that Cyrus restored the vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken to Babylon.
- Titus is described as taking the Temple's treasures to Rome, so an item continuously in use from the First Temple could reach Rome that way.
- The difficulty is real, which is why the question of whether it was the First or Second Temple's curtain arises at all.
- I can't verify the precise Tosafot text, so check the Tosafot inside.

## The Pshat of the Question
Your question is a good one. The Babylonians took vessels in 586 BCE, and Jeremiah 52 and II Kings 25 list items taken or broken up. A First Temple paroches would then have to survive centuries of exile and conquest to reach Rome.

## Possible Resolutions

### 1. Cyrus's return of the vessels
Ezra 1:7-11 says Cyrus "brought out the vessels of the House of the Lord that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem," and the count is given as 5,400. Even if the Babylonians took the paroches, it could have been returned and used in the Second Temple. Later it would have been taken to Rome with the other spoils, which is the tradition about Titus (Gittin 56b describes him taking the paroches).

### 2. Not everything was taken to Babylon
Some items may have been hidden or left behind, as the Gemara says of the Ark (Yoma 52b). A cloth is a different matter, though, and its survival over centuries is harder to explain.

### 3. Why one might say it was the Second Temple
The simpler reading is that R. Elazar b. R. Shimon was a late Tanna living after the destruction of the Second Temple. He saw spoils of the Temple that the Romans had actually destroyed. This is why the First Temple option needs an explanation like the one above.

## Further Considerations
- The Gemara (Yoma 21b) lists what was missing in the Second Temple: the Ark, the fire, the Shechina, *ruach hakodesh*, and the Urim VeTumim. That list does not include the paroches or the vessels, which fits the idea that those were returned.
- A cloth lasting four or five centuries is a practical difficulty, and that may be part of what pushes toward the Second Temple.

To pin down the machlokes, look at the Tosafot on Yoma 57a and any later commentary that discusses it. Tell me what the Tosafot says on your daf and I can help you work through it.

answer:
Your question could be read a few ways, so I've assumed you mean **what the Talmud itself is built from**. In short, the Talmud rests on Written Torah (Tanakh), the Oral Torah as taught in the **Mishnah** and **Baraitot**, and the discussions of the Amoraim, with later layers added by the Savoraim. If you meant something else, such as the Talmudic sources for a specific law or topic, tell me and I'll tailor the answer. No specific passages were retrieved, so this answer draws on my general knowledge.

## Key Takeaways

- The Talmud has two parts: the **Mishnah** (c. 200 CE, redacted by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) and the **Gemara** (the Amoraic discussion of it).
- The Gemara draws on **Tanakh**, **Baraitot** (Tannaitic teachings outside the Mishnah), and Tannaitic Midrashim.
- The Talmud also relies on received tradition (*Halacha LeMoshe MiSinai*), rabbinic enactments, and logical hermeneutic rules.
- There are two Talmuds: the **Bavli** (Babylonian) and the **Yerushalmi** (Jerusalem).

## The Core Layers

### 1. Written Torah (Tanakh)
The Gemara constantly asks *mena hani milei?* ("From where do we know this?") and grounds laws in verses. Not every law is derived this way. Some are only "hinted at" (*asmachta*) in the text.

### 2. The Mishnah
The Mishnah is the foundational text of the Oral Torah, arranged in six orders (*Sedarim*) and redacted by **Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi**. The Gemara is structured as commentary on it. Rav Sherira Gaon's *Iggeret* is the classic account of how it was compiled.

### 3. Baraitot and Tannaitic Collections
A **Baraita** is a Tannaitic teaching not included in the Mishnah. The Gemara often cites these as *tanya* or *tanu rabbanan* ("it was taught"). They come from collections such as:

- **Tosefta**, a parallel compilation to the Mishnah.
- **Midrash Halacha**: *Mekhilta* (Exodus), *Sifra* (Leviticus), and *Sifrei* (Numbers and Deuteronomy).

The Talmud notes that anonymous statements in these works reflect specific Sages: "an unattributed Mishnah is Rabbi Meir, an unattributed Tosefta is Rabbi Nechemya, an unattributed Sifra is Rabbi Yehuda, an unattributed Sifrei is Rabbi Shimon, and all follow Rabbi Akiva" [Sanhedrin 86a].

### 4. Hermeneutic Rules
The Sages derived law using interpretive principles such as *kal vachomer* (a fortiori reasoning) and *gezerah shavah* (verbal analogy). These are traditionally listed as Hillel's seven rules and Rabbi Yishmael's thirteen.

### 5. Received Tradition and Rabbinic Enactments
- ***Halacha LeMoshe MiSinai***: laws transmitted orally from Sinai without a scriptural source.
- ***Gezeirot* and *takkanot***: protective decrees and enactments by the Sages.
- ***Minhag***: established custom.

### 6. Amoraic Discussion
The **Amoraim** (c. 200–500 CE) analyzed the Mishnah, reconciled contradictions between sources, and added their own rulings and aggadic teachings. The **Savoraim** and later editors gave the Bavli its final shape.

## Two Talmuds
- **Talmud Yerushalmi** was compiled in the Land of Israel, c. 400 CE.
- **Talmud Bavli** was compiled in Babylonia, c. 500 CE, and is the more authoritative and widely studied.

## Non-Legal Sources
Aggadah in the Talmud draws on stories, ethical maxims, folklore, medicine, and astronomy, and includes teachings of individual Sages.

answer:
Mishnah Yevamot 1:3 belongs to the opening unit of the tractate, which deals with the *ervah* (forbidden-relative) exemption from *yibbum* and *chalitzah*. I can't reproduce its exact wording from memory with confidence, and I don't want to invent a text or attribute positions to it that may be wrong. No sources were retrieved for this question, so everything below comes from my general knowledge of the tractate.

## Key Takeaways

- Yevamot 1:1-1:4 develops a single topic: when a forbidden relative (*ervah*) is married to one's brother, the brother's other wives (the *tzarot*) are also exempt from levirate obligations.
- The basic rule is that the forbidden wife is exempt, and her co-wives are exempt along with her.
- Mishnah 1:3 sits in the middle of this unit. It follows the list of 15 relatives (1:1) and the explanation of how the exemption works (1:2), and it leads into the Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel dispute about co-wives (1:4).
- The mishnah is best studied together with the Gemara on [Yevamot 3a-13b].

## The Background

**The Torah source:** [Deuteronomy 25:5-10] obligates a surviving brother to marry (*yibbum*) his deceased brother's childless widow, or to release her through *chalitzah*. The Gemara reads this as applying only when the widow is not otherwise forbidden to him by a prohibition such as incest [Yevamot 3a-b].

**The structure of the unit:**

- **1:1** lists 15 women whose co-wives are also exempt, such as a daughter, a granddaughter, a mother-in-law and a sister-in-law.
- **1:2** explains the mechanism. If one of these relatives is married to the deceased brother, she is forbidden to the surviving brother, so he cannot perform *yibbum* with her. The Mishnah rules that her co-wives are exempt too.
- **1:3 and 1:4** refine the rule. They address cases where the forbidden relative dies, is divorced, or otherwise leaves the picture, and they record the dispute between **Beit Shammai** and **Beit Hillel** over whether the co-wives are then permitted.

## The Underlying Logic

The central question is why a co-wife should be exempt because of someone else's prohibition. The Gemara bases the rule on the idea that the *ervah* "exempts" her co-wife because the marital bond is linked together (*zikah*). The case remains a single bond between the brother and the family, and it cannot be split so that one wife is bound by it while the other is not.

If you mean which tractate is quoted most in Jewish literature, the best-supported answer is **Pirkei Avot** in popular and liturgical use, with **Berakhot** as a strong candidate in halachic and liturgical sources. I'm not aware of a rigorous statistical study, so this comes from my general knowledge, not the retrieved sources.

## Key Takeaways

- The Torah itself doesn't quote the Mishnah; the Mishnah comments on and systematizes the Oral Torah that accompanies it.
- Within the Talmud, each tractate of Gemara is built around its own Mishnah, so the most-quoted tractate depends on how you count.
- **Pirkei Avot** is probably the most commonly quoted in sermons, books, and the siddur.
- **Berakhot** is heavily cited in halacha because it governs prayer, *Shema*, and blessings.

## Clarifying the Question

**Written Torah:** The Torah precedes the Mishnah, so the relationship runs the other way. The Mishnah and Talmud cite verses from the Torah.

**Tradition of Sinai:** The retrieved source from [Berakhot 5a] reads "וְהַמִּצְוָה — זוֹ מִשְׁנָה" ("and the commandment, this is Mishnah"), and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish concludes "שֶׁכּוּלָּם נִתְּנוּ לְמֹשֶׁה מִסִּינַי" ("that all of them were given to Moses at Sinai"). So the tradition sees the Mishnah as rooted in Sinai, even though it was redacted later.

## Possible Meanings of "Most Quoted"

### In the Talmud
Each tractate of the Bavli is organized around its Mishnah, so every tractate quotes its own Mishnah extensively. Larger tractates, such as **Shabbat**, **Eruvin**, **Pesachim**, and **Bava Batra**, contain more Mishnaic text simply because of their size. Cross-tractate citations also run through the Gemara, but I don't have numbers on which tractate is cited most from outside.

### In popular and liturgical use
- **Pirkei Avot** is quoted far more than any other tractate in books, divrei Torah, and ethics literature. It is also read on Shabbat afternoons between Pesach and Rosh Hashanah in many communities.
- **Berakhot** gives us the structure of the *Shema* and the *Amidah*. This connects to the source in the Rambam [Mishneh Torah, Prayer and the Priestly Blessing 1:1] on the obligation to pray daily.
- Fragments of the Mishnah also appear in the siddur, such as *Eizehu Mekoman* (Zevachim ch. 5) and *Bameh Madlikin* (Shabbat ch. 2).

### In halachic codes
The Shulchan Aruch and the Mishneh Torah draw on all of the Mishnah, but **Orach Chayim** (Shabbat, Berakhot, Pesachim, Sukkah) engages tractates relevant to daily life most often.

answer:
Understanding a *hava aminah* (the initial assumption) alongside the *maskanah* (the conclusion) shows what a Torah law is, what it is not, and why. The Gemara's rejected assumptions mark the boundaries of a concept, and the reasoning that overturns them often reveals principles that apply across many areas of Torah. Studying only the conclusion gives you the halacha; studying the *hava aminah* as well gives you the logic behind it.

*No specific sources were retrieved for this question, so everything below comes from my general knowledge of Talmudic method.*

## Key Takeaways

- A *hava aminah* is a reasonable assumption the Gemara considers and then rejects or refines, and it is not a mistake.
- The distance between the *hava aminah* and the *maskanah* defines the exact scope of a halacha.
- Many Talmudic disputes come from different understandings of what the *hava aminah* was, and which of its elements were rejected.
- Rishonim and Acharonim often build entire analytical frameworks (*lomdus*) on this contrast.
- Working through the rejected option sharpens your intuition for how the Gemara reasons.

## What the Terms Mean

The **Gemara** often introduces a position with "*hava amina...*" (I would have thought...), followed by "*mashma lan*" (it teaches us) or "*ha kamashma lan*" (this is what it teaches us). The *hava aminah* is the natural reading. The *maskanah* is where the argument lands after the analysis.

The *hava aminah* is not a straw man. Typically it rests on a real principle that holds in some other context. That is why it teaches so much.

## How the Contrast Creates Knowledge

### 1. It defines the *chiddush* (novelty)

A statement in a Mishnah or Baraita must teach something. Asking "What would I have thought without it?" reveals the innovation. For example, the Gemara frequently asks why a source needed to teach a case, and answers that without it we would have assumed the opposite. The *hava aminah* shows what the *chiddush* is.

### 2. It reveals the underlying principle

When the Gemara rejects an assumption, it usually names the principle that overrides it. A familiar pattern is the question of why a case is not treated like a similar one. Answering requires isolating the factor that distinguishes them, which is the *sevara* (logical reasoning) at the heart of the sugya.

### 3. It explains the *tzrichuta* (the need for two sources)

The Gemara often asks why the Torah needed to state two similar laws. The answer is usually that each one alone would have led to a *hava aminah* that only the other corrects. Tracing these assumptions shows how the sources limit one another and why neither is redundant.

### 4. It exposes the structure of machlokes

Two Amoraim or Rishonim may agree on the conclusion but differ on which part of the *hava aminah* was rejected. This produces different practical outcomes in related cases. Asking "what did the Gemara originally think, and which element fell away?" often explains why a Rishon rules differently in a nearby case.

## Why Acharonim Value It

Brisker *lomdus* and similar approaches often analyze a sugya by asking precisely what the Gemara first assumed and what changed. Distinguishing the *cheftza* (the object) from the *gavra* (the person) is a typical example. A rejected assumption may have treated the law as belonging to one category, and the conclusion moves it to the other. That reclassification can then explain many seemingly unrelated rulings.

## Practical Study Tips

- When you see "*hava amina*," pause and ask: **What principle makes this assumption reasonable?**
- Ask: **What exactly dislodges it?** Is it a verse, a logical distinction, or a precedent?
- Ask: **Is the assumption rejected entirely, or only narrowed?**
- Compare how Rashi, Tosafot, and later commentators read the original assumption. Their differences often reveal their whole approach to the sugya.
- Test the conclusion on new cases and ask whether the original assumption would have given a different answer.

## A Broader Theme

This method reflects a Torah idea that truth is reached through struggle with alternatives. The Gemara preserves the rejected views, which is why we study them at all. As Chazal teach about the debates of Beit Hillel and Beit Shammai, "these and these are the words of the living God" [Eruvin 13b]. Even the rejected path teaches something, because it clarifies the boundaries of the accepted one.

answer:
Ma'aser behema (the animal tithe) is discussed mainly in **Masechet Bekhorot, chapter 9**, beginning around **Bekhorot 53b** and running to the end of the tractate. The calendar for it, the "new year for animal tithes," is discussed in **Masechet Rosh Hashanah**. The retrieved passages (Deuteronomy 14:22-26 and 26:14) concern *ma'aser sheni* (second tithe) and grain, wine, and oil, not the animal tithe. The references below come from my general knowledge, not the retrieved sources.

## Key Takeaways

- The central sugya is Bekhorot, chapter 9 (from about 53b), which covers how the animal tithe is counted and brought.
- The source verse is Leviticus 27:32-33, not Deuteronomy 14.
- Rosh Hashanah (Mishnah 1:1 and its Gemara) discusses the cutoff date for each year's animal tithe, with Tannaim disagreeing between 1 Elul and 1 Tishrei.
- The mitzvah applies only to the Temple-era Land of Israel setting, so it has no practical application today.

## The Biblical Source

The Torah commands that every tenth animal "that passes under the rod" is holy to God: "וְכׇל־מַעְשַׂר בָּקָר וָצֹאן כֹּל אֲשֶׁר־יַעֲבֹר תַּחַת הַשָּׁבֶט הָעֲשִׂירִי יִהְיֶה־קֹּדֶשׁ לַיהוָה" ("Every tithe of herd or flock, whatever passes under the rod, the tenth shall be holy to the Lord") [Leviticus 27:32]. Verse 33 adds that the owner may not inspect or substitute the animal.

Deuteronomy 14:23 mentions the firstborn (*bekhorot*) of herd and flock beside the tithes of grain, wine, and oil. This is why the topic is often studied near Bekhorot, but the animal tithe itself is a separate obligation.

## Main Talmudic Locations

- **Bekhorot, chapter 9 (c. 53b onward):** This is the main discussion. It covers how the animals are gathered into a pen and let out one by one, with every tenth marked. It also covers what happens if the count goes wrong, and how the tithe is eaten and its blood offered.
- **Bekhorot, c. 58b:** This section explores the phrase "passes under the rod" (*tachat ha-shevet*) and the mechanics of counting.
- **Rosh Hashanah, Mishnah 1:1 and the Gemara (c. 2a-8a, 12a):** This discusses the "new year" for animal tithes. The Mishnah rules it is 1 Elul, following R. Meir, while R. Elazar and R. Shimon say 1 Tishrei. Animals born in different tithing years cannot be combined in one count.
- **Temurah and Me'ilah:** These touch on the tithe's sanctity, substitution, and misuse of consecrated property.

## Why the Rosh Hashanah Discussion Matters

Each tithing year is a separate unit, so the Gemara needs a clear boundary date. The disagreement turns on when the animal-gathering season of the year ends. This parallels the other "new years" in the same Mishnah, such as the ones for kings and for tree tithes.

answer:
Chapter 1 of **Semachot** (also called *Evel Rabbati*, "the Great Mourning") deals mainly with the status of a *goses* (a person in the final stages of dying) and with the line between the living, the dead, and those not formally mourned, such as a stillborn infant. Only part of this is covered in the retrieved sources, so I note below what comes from them and what comes from my own knowledge of the tractate. Chapter divisions and wording differ among manuscripts and editions (Higger, Zlotnick), so verify the details against your edition.

## Key Takeaways

- A *goses* is legally **"like a living person in all respects"** (*harei hu ke-chai le-khol davar*), so nothing may be done that hastens death.
- Many ordinary post-death acts, such as closing the eyes or binding the jaw, are forbidden until death is certain.
- The chapter also establishes categories of people for whom **full mourning is not observed**, including a stillborn infant.
- The retrieved Sefer Puah passage rules that a baby born dead, even after nine months or born in pieces, is not mourned or eulogized, citing [Rambam, via Sefer Puah, Pregnancy and Birth, Miscarriages 63:48, citing Semachot ch. 1].
- Mourning is regulated by Torah limits, as in [Deuteronomy 14:1], which forbids excessive grief.

## The Goses (from my knowledge of the tractate, not the retrieved sources)

The tractate opens with the laws of the dying person. The core principle is that a goses is considered fully alive, so one may not tie his jaws, close his eyes, move him, or begin burial preparations before death occurs.

The classic image is a flickering candle: touching it can extinguish it. The tractate says that one who closes the eyes of a goses as the soul departs is "shedding blood," meaning he is hastening death. This is the source of later halachic discussion in [Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 339], which also deals with the limits of intervention at the end of life.

The chapter also treats the period just after death, specifying what may be done and when. This shows the tractate's concern that mourning practices never override the sanctity of life.

## Who Is Not Mourned (from the retrieved source)

The Sefer Puah passage rests on Semachot ch. 1. Its Hebrew reads: "תינוק שנולד מת... אין מתאבלים עליו ואין מספידים אותו" ("A baby born dead... is not mourned and is not eulogized"). This holds even if the baby was born after nine full months or emerged "מחותך או מרוסס" (cut up or crushed). [Sefer Puah, 63:48, citing Rambam, and Semachot ch. 1]

The logic is that a child who never lived outside the womb has not entered the halachic category of one who "died." Mourning (*aveilut*) applies to someone who lived and then died. Related rules for infants who lived fewer than thirty days (a *nefel*/non-viable child) are discussed in the tractate and later in [Rambam, Hilchot Evel 1] and [Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 374].

## Why Torah Limits Mourning

[Deuteronomy 14:1] says: "בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַיהֹוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם לֹא תִתְגֹּדְדוּ וְלֹא־תָשִׂימוּ קָרְחָה בֵּין עֵינֵיכֶם לָמֵת" ("You are children of the Lord your God; you shall not gash yourselves or make a bald patch between your eyes for the dead"). The Sages read this broadly as a framework in which grief is real but disciplined. Semachot builds on this by defining exactly when and for whom mourning begins.

## Underlying Themes

- **Sanctity of life:** Even a dying person's remaining moments of life must be protected.
- **Precision in categories:** Halacha needs clear definitions of life, death, and mourning status.
- **Dignity and restraint:** Mourning honors the dead without crossing into forbidden excess.

answer:
The retrieved passages don't include this Semachot text, so what follows is my own reconstruction and not a verified quotation. The dispute most likely turns on whether the eulogy is *true* for such a person. Rabbi Yehuda appears to hold that "righteous" and "his own hands" cannot truthfully describe a slave, or a non-Jew who isn't bound by Torah law. The Sages likely allow it because honest labor and decency are praiseworthy in anyone.

## Key Takeaways

- The retrieved sources (Deut. 14:1, Lev. 10:6, Sefer Puah) do not address this dispute, so the explanation below comes from general knowledge.
- Eulogies (*hespedim*) must be truthful, so the question is whether each phrase fits the deceased.
- A slave's earnings legally belong to his master, so "the labor of his own hands" is problematic for a slave [Gittin 12a; Kiddushin 23b].
- "Righteous" (*tzaddik*) may imply Torah observance, which is a problem for a non-Jew or a slave with limited obligations.
- The Sages likely take a broader view: moral integrity and honest work deserve recognition, and honoring the dead promotes peace (*darkei shalom*).

## Detailed Analysis

### The likely points of tension

The phrase has two parts, and each may be the root of the disagreement.

- **"A righteous man"**: In Jewish usage, a *tzaddik* is typically someone who fulfills God's commandments. A slave has reduced obligations, and a non-Jew is bound only by the Noahide laws. Rabbi Yehuda may therefore see the term as inaccurate or inappropriate.
- **"Who lived by the labor of his own hands"**: This praises self-sufficiency. A Canaanite slave's work and earnings belong to his master [Kiddushin 23b], so the praise may be untrue of him. For a non-Jew, however, it could be entirely accurate.

### Possible reasoning for the Sages

The Sages likely hold that "righteous" can be used in a general moral sense, meaning honest and upright, without implying full Torah observance. The Torah itself recognizes righteous non-Jews. The Sages also teach that we tend to a non-Jew's dead "for the sake of peace" [Gittin 61a]. Praising real virtue fits that principle.

### Why they disagree

The underlying question is whether a eulogy's wording is judged by its technical halachic meaning or by its ordinary moral meaning. If the former, Rabbi Yehuda's caution makes sense. If the latter, the Sages' leniency does.

### Caveat

I cannot confirm which Sage holds which position, or the precise wording and structure of the baraita. Please check the text of *Semachot* 1 directly, or in the Higger edition with commentary, to see which reasoning the text itself supports.

answer:
Yes, but indirectly. The Talmud never spells out a formal "Yissachar-Zevulun partnership" contract. Its basis is the Torah's pairing of the two tribes (Genesis 49:13-15, Deuteronomy 33:18), the Sifrei and Midrash's reading of that pairing, and Talmudic passages that praise and reward those who support Torah scholars. The classic partnership model is mainly a feature of Midrash, Rishonim, and later halachic literature.

## Key Takeaways

- The Torah pairs Zevulun and Yissachar in Moses' blessing: "Rejoice, Zevulun, in your going out, and Yissachar in your tents" (Deut. 33:18).
- The explicit "partnership" reading comes from Midrash (Sifrei, Bereishit Rabbah, Tanchuma), not from a Talmudic ruling.
- The Talmud provides related principles: supporting Torah scholars is valued, and the Torah scholar's merit is shared with the supporter.
- Halachic authorities (e.g., Rema) cite the arrangement as a legitimate and praiseworthy practice.
- The Zohar's description of Yissachar and Zevulun as the "two thighs" (Zohar, Mishpatim 3:200) shows the Kabbalistic version of the same idea: a structural support for Torah.

## The Biblical Foundation (Pshat)

Jacob blessed Zevulun as dwelling "at the shore of the seas" and as a "haven for ships" (Gen. 49:13). Yissachar is described as "a strong-boned donkey" who bends his shoulder to bear a burden (Gen. 49:14-15). The text itself does not state that one supports the other.

Moses' blessing joins them: "Rejoice, Zevulun, in your going out, and Yissachar in your tents." The Midrash reads "going out" as commerce and "tents" as Torah study, with the two tribes working together.

## Where the Partnership Idea Appears

- **Midrash**: Sources such as Sifrei on Deuteronomy 33 and Bereishit Rabbah 99 explain that Zevulun engaged in trade and supported Yissachar, who studied Torah. Rashi on Deuteronomy 33:18 reflects this reading. I am citing this from my general knowledge rather than from the retrieved passages, so please verify the exact wording.
- **Zohar**: The retrieved passage calls Yissachar and Zevulun "two thighs," a place "where the true prophets nurse." It quotes "And of the children of Yissachar, men who understood the times" (1 Chron. 12:33) and "Rejoice, Zevulun in your going out." Here the pairing is a structural, spiritual support. [Zohar, Mishpatim 3:200]

## Talmudic Parallels

The Talmud supplies the underlying values rather than the formal arrangement:

- **Supporting Torah scholars**: Ketubot 111b discusses cleaving to the Sages through supporting them. It asks how one can cleave to the Divine Presence, and answers that one should marry one's daughter to a scholar and do business on behalf of scholars. This is probably the closest Talmudic basis for the idea.
- **Shared reward**: Berakhot 63b and related passages stress the great value of those who support Torah study. Pesachim 53b tells of Rabbi Akiva's teaching about the benefit of connection to scholars, though this too is a general principle.
- **Torah and work**: Avot 2:2 ("Excellent is Torah study together with a worldly occupation") and Berakhot 35b (the dispute between Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and Rabbi Yishmael about how to balance Torah and labor) show the Talmud's tension over this question. The partnership model is one practical resolution of that tension.

Note that I am citing these from memory, and the exact application of some of them to the Yissachar-Zevulun model is my own framing.

## Halachic Development

Later authorities treat the arrangement as legitimate. The **Rema** (Yoreh De'ah 246:1) records a practice of supporting Torah study in exchange for a share in the reward. There is a halachic discussion about whether the supporter genuinely receives a portion of the scholar's merit, and about how the financial terms should be structured. Some authorities raise concerns about whether the scholar may "sell" his Torah, and about the terms of such a contract.

## Why the Question Is Subtle

The tension is between two ideals. One is that Torah should not be used as a "spade to dig with" (Avot 4:5), meaning it should not be a livelihood. The other is that communal support of scholars is highly meritorious. The partnership model is widely accepted, but how it is structured is debated.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
The Mishnah contains **517 perakim** (chapters) across its 63 tractates (*masechtot*), according to the standard count. This is the count in the commonly printed Mishnah, which divides the work into six orders (*sedarim*). Note that "Shas Mishnayot" is the Mishnah itself, not the Talmud, and the retrieved sources do not address this count, so what follows comes from my general knowledge.

## Key Takeaways

- The standard count is **517 perakim** in **63 masechtot** across **6 sedarim**.
- Some counts differ slightly (for example, 523 in some lists) because of how tractates are divided or combined.
- The Talmud Bavli discusses only 37 of the 63 masechtot, so the number of perakim in the Bavli differs from the Mishnah.
- The Mishnah is organized by *seder* (order), *masechet* (tractate), *perek* (chapter), and *mishnah* (paragraph).

## Breakdown by Seder (standard count)

- **Zeraim** (agricultural laws): 11 tractates, 74 perakim
- **Moed** (festivals): 12 tractates, 88 perakim
- **Nashim** (family law): 7 tractates, 71 perakim
- **Nezikin** (damages and civil law): 10 tractates, 73 perakim
- **Kodashim** (sacrifices): 11 tractates, 90 perakim
- **Tohorot** (purity): 12 tractates, 126 perakim

These add up to 522 in this tally, which shows the real-world variation. Many lists give 517 because they count Bava Kamma, Bava Metzia, and Bava Batra as a single tractate, *Nezikin*, in some traditions, or treat Makkot and Sanhedrin differently. Figures also vary by edition, since some editions split or merge chapters, and by whether Tractate Kinnim and Middot are counted fully.

## Why the Numbers Vary

- **Tractate divisions:** Some traditions treat the three "Bava" tractates as one unit, and Sanhedrin-Makkot as a single unit, which changes the totals.
- **Edition differences:** Manuscripts and printings divide chapters slightly differently, a point that also comes up in the Talmudic commentators' discussions of how to divide a text into *perakim*.
- **Mishnah vs. Gemara:** The Bavli has 2,711 pages (dapim) over 37 tractates, and its chapters follow the Mishnah's divisions.

I'd suggest verifying the exact figure against the edition you are learning from, as sources cite both 517 and slightly different totals depending on the counting method.

## Key Takeaways

- The man is anonymous in the Gemara [Sanhedrin 75a].
- He fell dangerously ill from his desire for a particular woman, and the doctors said only relations with her could cure him.

## The Story

A man became overwhelmed with desire for a woman, and his condition became life-threatening. The doctors said he would not recover unless he had relations with her.

The Sages answered that he should die rather than do this. The case is then narrowed through a series of proposals, each rejected:

- Could she stand before him naked? No.
- Could she speak with him from behind a fence? No.

He died rather than be cured through a forbidden act.

## The Reasons Given

The Gemara records two explanations:

- **Rav Yaakov bar Idi** (or according to some versions, the discussion centers on the woman's marital status) says she was a married woman.
- **Rav Acha** says she was unmarried, and the Sages still refused, so that Jewish women would not be treated carelessly in matters of sexual morality (*parutzin*, laxity). The Gemara frames this as a matter of public standards, not only the individual case.

I am recalling the attribution of specific names to these opinions from memory, so check the page inside to confirm them.

## Halachic Context

The story appears in the discussion of *yehareg v'al ya'avor* (be killed rather than transgress), which applies to the three cardinal sins: idolatry, forbidden relations, and murder. It illustrates that even a medical danger caused by desire does not override the prohibition on forbidden relations. Later codifiers such as the Rambam apply this principle.

answer:
The primary source is **Yevamot 63a**, which teaches that calamity comes to the world on account of Israel, so that Israel will take note and repent. It cites **Tzefaniah 3:6-7**, where Hashem says He cut off nations and destroyed their towers, and then says "I said: Surely you will fear Me, you will accept correction." No sources were retrieved for this question, so everything below comes from my own knowledge of the tradition.

## Key Takeaways

- **Yevamot 63a** says that "no calamity comes to the world except because of Israel," citing Tzefaniah 3:6-7.
- The plain meaning of the verse is that Hashem shows destruction among the nations as a warning for Israel to learn from.
- **Rambam, Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:1-3** teaches that one should not dismiss misfortune as mere chance, but should see it as a call to examine one's deeds.
- Learning a lesson from others' tragedies does not mean gloating or claiming to know the specific cause of any event.

## The Sources

### Tzefaniah 3:6-7
**הִכְרַתִּי גוֹיִם נָשַׁמּוּ פִּנּוֹתָם... אָמַרְתִּי אַךְ תִּירְאִי אוֹתִי תִּקְחִי מוּסָר**
"I have cut off nations, their corners are desolate... I said: Surely you will fear Me, you will accept correction."

The point is that Hashem brings desolation upon the nations as a lesson. Israel is meant to absorb it and mend its ways.

### Yevamot 63a
The Gemara states: **אין פורענות באה לעולם אלא בשביל ישראל**, "Calamity comes to the world only on account of Israel." It then brings the verse from Tzefaniah as proof. Rashi and later commentators read this as saying that the purpose of such events is to awaken Israel to repent. This is often paired with the verse **"Shamu amim yirgazun"** (Exodus 15:14), which describes the nations trembling at what Hashem did.

### Rambam, Hilchot Ta'aniyot 1:1-3
Rambam does not cite the Tzefaniah passage directly, but he sets out the principle. When trouble comes, one should cry out and sound the alarm. Treating it as "the way of the world" or coincidence is called *achzariyut*, cruelty, because it prevents people from doing teshuva. The tragedy should prompt introspection.

### Related: Sukkah 29a
The Gemara discusses astronomical omens, such as eclipses, as signs for the nations or for Israel. This reflects the same idea that events in the wider world carry messages worth noticing.

## Important Caveats

- **Humility about causes:** Nothing here permits declaring that a particular tragedy happened for a particular sin. That kind of claim is generally discouraged, since we lack prophecy.
- **No gloating:** Chazal warn against rejoicing at others' suffering. Proverbs 24:17 says, "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls." Megillah 10b records that Hashem rebuked the angels for singing while the Egyptians drowned. The lesson is meant to move us inward, toward our own teshuva, rather than toward judging others.
- **Compassion:** Seeing others suffer should also awaken empathy and prayer.

For personal guidance, consult your local rabbi or posek.

answer:
The statement comes from **Gittin 59b**, which says that "great is peace," since the whole Torah was given *mipnei darchei shalom* ("for the sake of the ways of peace"), based on Proverbs 3:17: "Its ways are ways of pleasantness, and all its paths are peace." It means that peace is the Torah's overall purpose and the lens through which its laws are meant to function in the world. It does not mean every mitzvah is literally about avoiding conflict. (The 59b passage is cited from my own knowledge, not the retrieved passages, which come from the surrounding sugya.)

## Key Takeaways

- The proof-text is Proverbs 3:17, which describes the Torah's *derachim* (ways) as *noam* (pleasant) and its *netivot* (paths) as *shalom*.
- *Darchei shalom* is also a specific halachic category, used for particular rabbinic enactments to prevent strife.
- The broad statement presents peace as the Torah's goal, while the narrow category applies that goal to concrete cases.
- Rambam codifies the broad statement, saying the whole Torah was given to make peace in the world [Rambam, Hilchot Chanukah 4:14].

## Detailed Answer

### Two Different Uses of "Darchei Shalom"

The Mishnah opens a list with "These are things instituted *mipnei darchei shalom*": the Kohen reads first, then the Levi, then the Yisrael, and an *eruv* may be made in an old house [Gittin 59a, Mishnah]. These are specific, rabbinic-level arrangements.

The statement that "the whole Torah" is for darchei shalom is a different claim. It does not say that all laws are enactments of this type. It says that the Torah as a whole aims at a harmonious world, which is why the sugya places it right after the Mishnah's list.

### The Pshat of the Verse

Proverbs 3:17 speaks of the Torah itself: "Its ways are ways of pleasantness, and all its paths are peace." The Gemara reads this as a statement about the Torah's essential character. A Torah observed properly produces pleasant conduct and peaceful relations.

### The Practical Application: Gittin 61a

Our sugya gives a concrete case: "We do not protest against non-Jewish poor who take *leket*, *shikhecha*, and *pe'ah*, *mipnei darchei shalom*." The Gemara continues that we support non-Jewish poor along with Jewish poor, visit their sick, and bury their dead [Gittin 61a]. This shows how the principle works. Strict Torah law might not require this treatment, but peaceful relations in society call for it.

Many later authorities, notably the **Meiri** (from my own knowledge), stress that these obligations reflect real moral and social values, not mere political expedience.

### Why It Matters

The principle also affects how we read halacha:

- Some rabbinic enactments exist specifically to prevent quarrels, such as the order of aliyot.
- Halachic reasoning is expected to take social harmony into account.
- Even mitzvot that look rigorous operate within a Torah whose purpose is *shalom*.

There is a real tension here. The Torah includes laws of war and judicial punishment that do not look peaceful on the surface. The usual answer is that peace means a just and stable order, not just the absence of conflict, and that these laws serve that order. This is an interpretive point from tradition, not an explicit statement in the retrieved passages.

answer:
The teaching is that a judge must decide each case with the sober awareness that his ruling carries life-and-death, eternal consequences. He should picture a sword resting between his thighs and *Gehinnom* (the place of purgation) open beneath his feet. The images are meant to instill *yirat shamayim* (fear of Heaven) and to keep him from carelessness, favoritism, or judging out of fear or convenience.

I am quoting this teaching from memory of the tradition, not from the retrieved passage. The only retrieved source is Deuteronomy 16:20, and I am not certain of the exact masechet and daf of the Talmudic wording, so verify it inside before citing it.

## Key Takeaways

- The image of the sword and Gehinnom expresses the gravity of judging: a mistaken ruling can destroy an innocent person or wrongly enrich another.
- The judge is accountable not only to the litigants but to God, who is present in the court.
- Deuteronomy 16:20, "*Tzedek, tzedek tirdof*" ("Justice, justice shall you pursue"), sets the standard of relentless, diligent pursuit of truth.
- The fear is meant to produce careful deliberation, not paralysis. The judge must still judge.

## The Plain Meaning of the Image

The **sword** between the thighs is a picture of constant, immediate danger. The Rabbis tie it to the verse describing the guards of Solomon's bed, each "with his sword upon his thigh because of fear in the night" [Song of Songs 3:8]. The judge is likewise to keep a "fear in the night" in mind: a sense that something is at stake which he cannot see.

**Gehinnom open beneath him** adds the sense of ultimate accountability. A judge who perverts justice does not merely err; he risks a spiritual fall. Your phrase about "feet together" is best read as a judge standing on precarious ground, with one wrong step meaning disaster.

## The Judge Stands Before God

This teaching rests on a broader idea in the tradition: the court is a place where God is present.

- **Psalms 82:1** says, "*Elohim* stands in the congregation of God; in the midst of the judges He judges." The Rabbis read the first *Elohim* as referring to God Himself, present in the court.
- **Deuteronomy 1:17** says, "Fear not the face of man, for the judgment is God's." A judge's ruling is therefore a divine matter.
- **II Chronicles 19:6** has Jehoshaphat charge the judges: "See what you do, for you judge not for man but for the Lord."

The sword and Gehinnom are the vivid, personal form of this principle.

## Connection to *Tzedek, Tzedek Tirdof*

The retrieved verse reads: "צֶדֶק צֶדֶק תִּרְדֹּף לְמַעַן תִּחְיֶה וְיָרַשְׁתָּ אֶת־הָאָרֶץ" ("Justice, justice you shall pursue, so that you may live and inherit the land which the Lord your God gives you") [Deuteronomy 16:20].

- The verb *tirdof* (pursue) implies effort and persistence. Justice does not simply happen; the judge must chase it.
- The verse ties justice to national survival: "so that you may live and inherit the land." A corrupt court threatens the community's very existence.
- The repetition of *tzedek* is explained in the Talmud in several ways. One reading is that it points to pursuing justice by both strict law and compromise (*peshara*) [Sanhedrin 32b]. Another is that one should seek out the best court.

The fear of the sword and Gehinnom is the inner counterpart of this outward pursuit.

## Why the Fear Matters

- **It counters bias.** Bribery, social pressure, and sympathy for the poor or deference to the powerful all distort judgment. Fear of Heaven is the safeguard when no human can check the judge.
- **It encourages thoroughness.** A judge who feels the weight of his decision will examine the facts and law carefully.
- **It is balanced by duty.** The Talmud also warns that a judge who is capable should not shirk the role out of fear. The judge is told, in effect, to "be afraid" but still to rule on what his eyes see, since he has only what is before him.

For this reason the tradition calls a judge who rules truthfully a partner with God in the act of creation [Shabbat 10a], showing the other side of the same coin: the role carries both extraordinary danger and extraordinary merit.

- **Bereishit Rabbah 9:7** says that without the *yetzer*, no one would build a house, marry, or have children.
- A reasonable reading is that the *yetzer* can't be neatly split into a "bad" desire and a "good" desire, because the same drive underlies both.
- Humans were created to be channelers of desire, not beings without it.

## The Story Itself

The Gemara describes the Men of the Great Assembly (*Anshei Knesset HaGedolah*) praying to have the *yetzer* for idolatry handed over, and it was. They then sought the *yetzer* for forbidden relations (*arayot*). They imprisoned it for three days and found no fresh egg in all of Eretz Yisrael. They realized they couldn't kill it, and since Heaven doesn't grant half-requests, they blinded it. A parallel appears in **Sanhedrin 64a**.

The conclusion is not that people would stop obeying halacha. It is that reproduction would stop altogether, because the underlying drive would be gone.

## A Small Clarification on Rashi

You mention that the hens stopped laying because their reproductive system was removed. As I recall, Rashi's point is closer to the loss of the desire and drive that propels reproduction, not a physical removal. Please check Rashi inside, since I'm quoting from memory.

This matters for your question. If the loss is of the *drive* and not of the physical capacity, then the hens' case tells us that the *yetzer* is not an add-on to nature but part of how nature runs.

## Why Not Rely on the Tzaddikim?

### 1. The *yetzer* is the engine, not only the temptation
**Bereishit Rabbah 9:7**, on "*vehinei tov me'od*" ("and behold, it was very good"), says this refers to the *yetzer hara*, because without it no one would build a house, take a wife, have children, or engage in business. It also cites Kohelet 4:4, that all labor and skill come from a person's rivalry with his fellow. The *yetzer* here is the basic force of human desire and ambition.

Applied to your question, a tzaddik's responsible procreation is still fueled by the same underlying drive. Take it away and even a righteous person would lack the desire to marry and have children. A drive that is entirely absent can't be replaced by simply deciding to follow the mitzvah.

### 2. The mitzvah doesn't create the capacity
The Torah commands *pru urvu* (be fruitful and multiply), but a command presupposes a person able to act on it. The Gemara may be assuming that the physical and emotional capacity for marital relations depends on the drive that was removed. A mitzvah regulates desire but doesn't generate it. Halacha channels the *yetzer*, as with *onah* and permitted relations, but needs it to exist first.

### 3. The world was not designed for angels
A recurring Jewish idea, found in *Chazal* and later thought, is that the human task is to refine and direct the *yetzer*, not to eliminate it. The Gemara's own conclusion, to blind it but not kill it, matches this. Rashi, as I recall, takes the blinding to mean that the *yetzer* no longer powerfully draws a person toward the most forbidden relations (such as relatives) while still functioning in permitted ones. Verify this wording in Rashi directly.

### 4. Not everyone is a tzaddik
Your suggestion assumes that enough responsible tzaddikim would exist to sustain the world. Practically, though, the Gemara speaks of the whole world, and Zechariah's warning is about the survival of the species. A system depending only on exceptional people is not a stable design.

## Where to Look for Explicit Discussion

I'd recommend checking these for direct treatment, without claiming they all address your exact question:

- **Maharsha** on Yoma 69b and Sanhedrin 64a.
- **Iyun Yaakov** and **Ein Yaakov** commentaries (such as Ben Yehoyada) on the aggadah.
- **Maharal**, who writes often on the *yetzer hara* as a necessary part of creation.
- **Rav Dessler** (*Michtav MeEliyahu*) and other *mussar* writers on the role of desire.

If you tell me which edition or commentary you're using, I can help you work through the specific text.
